title: How Direct Instruction — and Its Blowback — Radicalized Me
author: Kevin Huffman
summary: Kevin Huffman responds to season two of the Sold a Story podcast, which follows the development of direct instruction and its advocate Siegfried Engelmann, by recalling his own start as a 22-year-old bilingual first grade teacher in Houston in 1992. His principal, Ramon Alvarez, brought direct instruction into the school after seeing results at Wesley Elementary, and the people interviewed in the podcast were his trainers and colleagues. His students did very well in reading and math in Spanish and English, yet the school was swept into three edu-wars at once over phonics, direct instruction and bilingual transition, and visitors from the university and district disliked what they saw. Huffman uses the story to raise a meta problem: why do adults block what works for children, and why are decisions based on what adults like to do rather than on evidence. His conclusion is that decisions made on how adults feel can harm students, especially poor students, and that the Engelmann rule that if the child has not learned it, the teacher has not taught it, shaped his career.
points: Huffman's own early-career experience with direct instruction in Houston is the lens for the podcast's story of a method that worked but was resisted by education school orthodoxy.
His students read and did math above grade level in both Spanish and English, while visitors from the university and district argued about the method.
The meta question is why adults act as gatekeepers on practices that work for children when evidence should guide decisions.
Decisions made around adult preferences, such as autonomy or the look of a classroom, can harm poor students whose life outcomes depend on instruction.
The Engelmann principle that if the kid hasn't learned it, the teacher hasn't taught it put responsibility for success on the adults.
quotes: In a weird twist of circumstance, I knew all of these people when I was 22 years old, and just starting my career in education. Sold a Story essentially retraces my experience as a new teacher in the Houston Independent School District.
I was thrilled that experts were offering to help me do something that was backed up by evidence. I was an early adopter in the school — maybe the earliest adopter.

We were instead swept into three edu-wars at once: our reading methods were phonics-driven and cut against the favored “whole language” principles (see Sold a Story Season 1). Our instructional techniques that relied on direct instruction didn’t embrace autonomy and student discovery (Season 2). And we were flying in the face of accepted practice for bilingual students’ transition to English (maybe that can be Season 3). In short, nothing that we were doing matched the education school orthodoxy.
But the kids could really, really read, better than their peers in other schools. They could do math, consistently above grade level.

Why, if something works for kids, do we let adults prevent it from being implemented? Why do we make decisions on teaching and learning based on what adults like to do, rather than what evidence shows works for students?

Delivering a scripted curriculum sometimes feels bad to people, removing some level of professional autonomy. Teaching via books with giant letters and short boring sentences can seem less exciting than using an immersive and colorful big book. Embracing student discovery can seem more progressive than instructing students explicitly.

But when we make our decisions based on how adults feel, we can harm students. For students who are poor, these choices can literally inhibit their life outcomes. The decisions could not have higher consequences.
He really believed that all kids could learn. If the kid hasn’t learned it, the teacher hasn’t taught it. That was our basic rule.
